items.summary: Continual reinforcement learning (CRL) requires agents to operate under environmental changes while reusing prior knowledge whenever possible. We argue that model-based reinforcement learning provides a promising framework for this setting because learned world models (WMs) can, in principle, support change detection, knowledge reuse, adaptation, and acquisition of new knowledge. However, such benefits depend heavily on whether the learned model can generalize beyond the contexts in which it was trained. In this work, we propose to formulate this problem with a contextual Markov decision process in which context is decomposed into behavioral and physical components. This view organizes continual WM learning into reuse, adaptation, and acquisition of new knowledge. As a first step, we study direct reuse when behavioral rules remain unchanged. Using Dyna-Q and TD-MPC in controlled FourRooms tasks, we find that zero-shot reuse can degrade substantially under physical-context changes and that this behavior depends strongly on the observation representation used by the WM. Additional ablation studies and latent-space diagnostics suggest that learned representations do not automatically provide the invariances needed for reuse. These results identify representation generalization as an important bottleneck for reliable world-model reuse in CRL.
items.title: Before We Adapt: The Zero-Shot Generalization Bottleneck in Continual World Models

items.summary: This Version 2.1 report places the Maxwell Mass Effect at the forefront of a coherent model for the Venusian atmosphere. The surface temperature is treated as the dependent variable required to support the atmospheric mass against gravity. Solar energy is captured in a shallow topside thermal heating pool, stored as potential energy, and returned to depth by organised descent in the polar vortices under conservation of angular momentum. The sulfuric-acid lifting condensation level (LCL) acts as the thermodynamic anchor (Dew-Point Anchor Hypothesis). A two-component radiative opacity lapse rate then fixes only the geometric separation between that LCL and the infrared emission level. Stochastic inverse modelling with a VIRA equatorial profile, hydrostatic integration and thermodynamic filters recovers a cloud base near 49.6 km, an emission level near 69.4 km at approximately 229 K, and a surface pressure of approximately 91.5 bar. An order-of-magnitude energy-budget test shows that the required polar mass flux lies within the range of observed vortex descent speeds. Version 2 adds a quantitative recirculation (recycle) test using existing Venusian meridional circulation wind data. Observed poleward flows of ~10–15 m s⁻¹ at cloud tops imply a hemispheric Hadley-cell mass flux of order 10¹¹ kg s⁻¹ and a full recirculation timescale of 1–2 weeks. This multi-cycle pathway resolves the apparent single-pass temperature-rise tension and brings the adiabatic signature into agreement with observed polar temperature contrasts of 15–50 K. The same boundary conditions can be satisfied by a conventional greenhouse calculation, but only the Maxwell framework supplies a structural explanation for the polar vortices themselves and a dynamically consistent energy pathway. A new Discussion section explains the changes from Version 1 and how they address independent criticisms of the energy-budget magnitude and the need for a discriminating quantitative test. Diagnostic figures from the inverse model and the recirculation test are included.
items.title: The Maxwell Mass Effect as a Model for the Venusian Atmosphere

items.summary: Web world models increasingly predict the consequences of candidate actions before agents act, yet a plausible predicted future does not necessarily support the correct safety decision. In a matched human evaluation of 3,000 predictions from ten frozen open models, 86.1% are judged semantically plausible. However, several models exhibit highly asymmetric authorisation behaviour, combining low false-safe execution with poor recall of clarifiable ASK cases and a strong preference for BLOCK. This motivates safety sufficiency: whether a predictive interface preserves and exposes the policy-decisive information required to distinguish actions that may be EXECUTED, require clarification through ASK, or should be BLOCKED. We introduce SafeWebWorld, a benchmark for evaluating safety sufficiency across five web-safety domains through action-conditioned futures, policy-decisive evidence, and policy-conditioned decisions. Under a controlled Security-Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning protocol, evidence preservation can improve substantially while authorisation-sensitive decisions deteriorate. To determine whether this deterioration reflects loss of authorisation-sensitive score structure or a failure of the decision readout, we introduce Latent Authorisation Recovery (LAR). Frozen-score recalibration reveals substantial but backbone-dependent recovery, while paired recovery provides only a modest additional gain. Yet within-family and matched-authorisation evaluations remain poor, showing that aggregate recoverability does not imply robust fine-grained authorisation behaviour. Overall, plausible prediction, evidence preservation, and aggregate recovery are each insufficient on their own to establish robust authorisation.
items.title: Beyond Plausible Prediction: Safety Sufficiency in Web World Models

items.summary: Latent world models allow reinforcement learning agents to learn policies from imagined trajectories, yet determining the optimal depth of model reliance remains a fundamental challenge. Fixed imagination horizons apply uniform prediction depths regardless of trajectory reliability, exposing target values to compounding model error or over-relying on critic approximations. We introduce density-guided bootstrap boundaries, a trajectory-dependent mechanism that adapts the depth of imagined returns using a score-informed relative density proxy. The proxy accumulates the estimated divergence of a score-corrected auxiliary field formed by a feature displacement network and a noise-conditioned score estimator along imagined paths. We propose two gating mechanisms: a hard boundary that halts return expansion at a discrete state, and a soft boundary that continuously shifts the return recursion toward critic bootstrapping. Both variants preserve boundary value estimates and apply corresponding survival weights to actor and critic losses. Formulated independently of specific dynamics models and instantiated within Dreamer V3, we prove that the resulting gated Bellman operator is a strict contraction mapping and that early bootstrapping monotonically reduces conditional target variance. We clarify the theoretical assumptions distinguishing our expansion proxy from exact path likelihoods. Across continuous-control tasks and Atari Pong, empirical evaluations show that dynamic boundary selection enhances sample efficiency and late-training performance over fixed-horizon and auxiliary-enabled baselines.
items.title: Density-Guided Bootstrap Boundaries for Latent World-Model Reinforcement Learning

items.summary: Robot perception is increasingly data driven, yet field data is slow, costly, and sometimes disruptive to collect. Video world models offer a cheaper source: seeded with real frames, they extend a recorded scene into new footage with the deployment's sensor, altitude, and environment. We ask whether such synthetic data matches the utility of real field data and whether detectors trained with it perform in the field. Seeding a 7B-parameter world model with wildlife drone video, we more than double the training set with curated frames. On held-out videos from the same drones, mAP@50--95 rises 4.3\% when these frames are added to real data and 10.3\% when they replace it, and up to 33.5\% on an urban benchmark. Although an expert rejects an estimated 87.5\% of generated clips, the data costs about \$1,100 of GPU time, against more than \$3,200 of field labor alone for a less useful real training set. Synthetic data thus shifts data costs from fieldwork to compute.
items.title: Dreams Are Cheaper Than Flights: Curated World-Model Data Improves Aerial Detection

items.summary: Test-time scaling (TTS) improves large language model agents by sampling and selecting among multiple candidate trajectories, but common realizations assume that these trajectories can be executed in parallel. This assumption breaks in realistic deployments, where enterprise workspaces and cloud services are shared and persistent, costly or infeasible to replicate, and actions may introduce irreversible side effects or cross-trajectory interference. Existing generative world models avoid direct execution, but typically compress environment state into a single prompt, limiting their ability to reliably simulate transitions under partial observability. Instead, we introduce Agentic World Modeling (AWM), which reformulates next-observation prediction as a multi-turn evidence-acquisition task. For each hypothetical action, an agentic simulator adaptively queries the real environment through safe read-only interfaces, reasons over the returned evidence, and uses executable computation to construct the resulting observation without mutating shared state. Integrated with trajectory-level TTS, AWM enables parallel exploration over a single shared environment. Across $τ$-bench, AppWorld, and OfficeBench, AWM outperforms a single-shot simulation baseline by 40.07% on average, and surpasses a trained world-model baseline by 12.36% on average. These results establish interactive, read-grounded simulation as a practical foundation for safe and scalable agentic test-time scaling in shared, non-resettable environments.
items.title: Agentic World Modeling for Agent Test-time Scaling without Environment Replica

items.summary: Learned world models ship as software components whose model versions, preprocessing, and test harnesses change between releases. Work on model updates already counts per-sample regressions, or negative flips, that an accuracy check hides. Two problems remain: a test can pass under one configuration and fail under another, and a harness fault can produce erroneous scores and wrong verdicts without a crash. We present TetraState, a regression-testing protocol for paired possible/impossible video tests. Each test runs under four fixed model-native configurations; its number of correct verdicts assigns one of four outcome classes. Inconclusive tests and failed executions are reported separately alongside the verdict rate. Revisions are compared by per-test outcome transitions, and the harness is versioned as part of the system under test. On all 506 IntPhys 2 Main tests and two heterogeneous systems, Cosmos 3 Nano and V-JEPA 2, two V-JEPA 2 harness revisions move modal accuracy by only 0.2 and 2.6 points yet change 11 and 214 test labels; in the second, accuracy rises although fewer tests are judged correctly, and 43 regressions keep the modal verdict, so a modal-verdict flip check misses them. These results outline a research agenda on configuration-level regression oracles for learned components.
items.title: One Verdict Is Not Enough: Regression Testing Learned World Models and Their Test Harnesses

items.summary: Human preferences change over time: an established preference may remain valid over time, become uncertain as context shifts, or be explicitly revised. Effective personalization requires conversational AI to adapt its response strategy to evolving preferences rather than relying on passive memory retrieval. We formalize this capability as adaptive personalization under epistemic uncertainty. A human preference study further confirms that people favor state-contingent response strategies as preference uncertainty changes. To evaluate whether language models mirror this adaptation, we create a multilingual benchmark spanning 250 personas, 5 languages, and 25K conversational turns that decouples strategy selection from response execution. Across eight closed- and open-weight models, we uncover a recognition-generation gap: models reliably identify appropriate strategies when selecting among candidate options, but collapse during open-ended generation, suffering a 35-46% drop in strategy calibration. Crucially, this failure is systematic: models default to exploit-first behavior, over-relying on existing preferences regardless of preference epistemic uncertainty. We show this failure is addressable: while prompting interventions fail, targeted training that supervises models' internal strategy representations toward state-conditional human preferences narrows the user acceptability generalization gap by a third on out-of-distribution personas and conversational styles.
items.title: Adaptive Personalization Under Preference Epistemic Uncertainty

items.summary: The ability to integrate new information and deduce its consequences is central to learning, understanding, and reasoning in large language models (LLMs). Whether information arrives during training or in-context, models must not only store local facts, but propagate their long-range implications globally. To explore information integration in LLMs, we introduce two complementary natural language benchmarks for large-scale evaluation of deductive reasoning as a function of inference depth. The first is a formal graph benchmark enabling controlled evaluation over a wide range of graph topologies and integration tasks; the second is a knowledge composition benchmark grounded in real-world knowledge graphs. We use these benchmarks to compare knowledge integration from information encoded in context versus information encoded in model weights during pretraining, evaluating a set of open models implicitly, without chain of thought. We find that accuracy decays sharply with increased composition length for both pretrained and in-context knowledge. Information presented in-context, however, substantially outperforms deduction over information encoded in weights. These results quantify a fundamental limitation of current models with direct implications for prompt-based control of agent behavior and for continual learning strategies, and they provide a foundation for developing training, prompting, and integration methods that support deeper reasoning.
items.title: ImplicitHop: Evaluating knowledge integration across context and memory

items.summary: Memory has become central to self-evolving LLM agents, which store and retrieve experience from past rollouts to guide future decisions. Existing systems represent this experience as free-form natural language and maintain it by rewriting, which fits tasks whose experience is narratable. However, in scientific discovery and optimization, experience is often a quantity measured by an oracle under a specific context. Rewriting it as text leaves no index for where a record should be, replaces a measurement with a description, and cannot express how interventions interact. To address this, we argue that agent memory for biomolecule optimization should instead be indexable, quantitative, and structured, and we introduce MEMIG. This memory construction framework realizes these three properties. In detail, MEMIG addresses each insight with a domain-grounded identifier and accumulates the quantitative effect measured by a property oracle, so that updates remain local and retrieval becomes an exact lookup. Next, MEMIG connects insights whose interventions are applied together and measures their epistasis by decomposing each evaluated set. Our results show that MEMIG improves performance in most settings across in silico antibody optimization tasks.
items.title: MEMIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization

items.summary: Natural-language skills enable large language model (LLM) agents to reuse procedures across tasks, yet most systems retrieve individual skills from a flat SkillBank without explicitly modeling the high-level strategy that governs their selection and use. We introduce TalentRL, a strategy-guided reinforcement learning framework for hierarchical routing over procedural memory. Coarse-grained talents represent recurring strategies for skill use, while fine-grained skills provide executable procedures. For each task, the policy model selects a talent that guides execution and softly prioritizes its associated skills during similarity-based retrieval. However, since task outcomes depend jointly on talent selection, retrieved skill context, and downstream execution, terminal rewards alone cannot isolate the contribution of the routing decision. TalentRL therefore trains talent routing with reward contrasts between rollouts of the same task under matched interventions on the talent-conditioned context, and optimizes downstream execution with group-relative advantages. Across seven open-domain and multi-hop question-answering benchmarks, talent-aware supervised fine-tuning improves average success rate by 7.53%, 6.71%, and 9.21% over the corresponding zero-shot baselines for Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B, respectively. Reinforcement learning further improves these SFT checkpoints by 7.58% to 9.32%, and TalentRL achieves the highest average success rate among all compared methods on all three backbones. On the agentic benchmarks ALFWorld and WebShop, TalentRL achieves the highest ALFWorld success rate (99.3%) and the highest WebShop score (90.7) among all compared methods.
items.title: TalentRL: Strategy-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Hierarchical Skill Routing

items.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation is becoming agentic. A search harness writes queries, reads results, reformulates, and decides when to stop. This largely solves accuracy: a harness with only BM25/grep and MiniMax M3 answers 85% of BrowseComp-Plus and 91% on multi-hop FRAMES in our runs, without compiled or vector indexes. It exposes a context problem: an undisciplined loop repeats queries, rereads documents, and fills the window with unused passages. The missing layer is knowledge compilation: a configurable ingestion pipeline where LLMs enrich documents with context no chunk contains alone--navigation hierarchies with claim-evidence leaves, entity graphs, timelines, mind maps, ontologies, wikis, and memory. Compilation is not a better retriever: under a competent harness, structural artifacts gave no detectable accuracy gain on FRAMES, and a PageIndex-style outline degraded at scale. It is a supply layer. A navigation tree whose leaves are claim-evidence pairs--the mechanism we measure--cuts query tokens by 91% when evidence suffices and adds 1.9% when it does not, a 38% average reduction; this implies a 2% break-even sufficiency rate and a measured rate near 43%. A decision gate cuts latency from 140 s to 30 s, though substitution's token saving is bought with retrieval rounds and carries its own latency cost. Other artifacts--ontology, graph, wiki, timeline, mind map, memory--pay off in deployment (governance, integration, onboarding, temporal orientation, continuity) where accuracy benchmarks cannot see them. We describe RAGFlow's pipeline and harness (open source at https://github.com/infiniflow/ragflow), which turns the loop into five disciplined stations and keeps the context entering the model the smallest sufficient set; together they form an agent-native database: a store that hands the agent compiled, governed context instead of a ranked list of passages.
items.title: Context as Infrastructure: Knowledge Compilation for Retrieval in Agentic Systems with Harnesses

items.summary: We address the inverse problem of reconstructing a meson parton distribution function (PDF) or parton distribution amplitude (PDA) at a fixed scale from a finite set of Mellin moments. At finite moment order this map is ill posed in the Hadamard sense: the moments do not determine a unique, stable pointwise $x$-dependence, and small data perturbations can produce large changes in the reconstruction. We regularize the problem by restricting the admissible function class through constraints justified by first principles---support on $x\in[0,1]$, endpoint vanishing, unit normalization, and, for the pion, the exact $x\leftrightarrow 1-x$ symmetry---and by complementing these hard constraints with differentiable penalties that suppress the spurious multiple maxima and central concavity changes typical of ill-posed inversions. We parameterize the unknown function with two interchangeable neural cores, a multilayer perceptron (MLP) and a Kolmogorov--Arnold network (KAN), and find that the KAN reconstructs the target distributions more accurately, most markedly in the asymmetric (kaon) case. We attribute this advantage to the locality of the B-spline basis underlying the KAN, which localizes corrections during moment matching and damps the global oscillations to which the MLP is prone. Benchmarks against synthetic targets, using both ten and five input moments, support these conclusions.
items.title: Reconstructing Meson Parton Distributions from Mellin Moments with Artificial Neural Networks

items.summary: Flapping-wing simulation must reconcile high-frequency wingbeat aerodynamics with the slower dynamics relevant to flight control and reinforcement learning. We present FlapSim, a modular open-source MuJoCo simulation platform that combines robot descriptions, wing geometry, and composable aerodynamic models in a deterministic simulation pipeline. Across $48$ held-out scenarios spanning frequency, gimbal, wind, frequency-step, gust, and cross-robot flat-plate regimes, we compare five reduced-order configurations operating at $1\,\text{ms}$ with a $50\,μ\text{s}$ quasi-steady blade-element reference. The built-in hover cycle-averaged baseline achieves a $67.51\times$ CPU speedup but only $0.6593$ mean wrench fidelity. Combining multirate $21$-substep clock synchronization, three-dimensional linear/quadratic inflow and gust coupling, analytical blade-element geometry scaling, and phase-locked $1f\text{--}6f$ harmonics raises mean fidelity to $0.9646$ at a $65.19\times$ speedup in a five-block model. A streamlined four-block model without explicit step-transient lag states achieves $0.9662$ fidelity at a $67.98\times$ speedup. Controlled ablations show that stroke harmonics are particularly important during frequency transitions, improving held-out frequency-step fidelity by $+0.3176$. Transfer-function analysis explains this effect: fixed-window cycle averaging retains harmonic contributions when the wingbeat frequency changes, so within-cycle reconstruction also improves the filtered wrench. Once phase alignment and harmonic synthesis are included, explicit transient lag states provide no additional benefit in this benchmark. These results characterize the accuracy--computation tradeoff of the aerodynamic hierarchy and identify timing, inflow, geometry, and harmonic representation as central considerations for reduced-order flapping-wing simulation.
items.title: FlapSim: A Composable MuJoCo Simulation Platform and Reduced-Order Aerodynamic Model Hierarchy for Flapping-Wing Robotics

items.summary: Resolution Geometry: A Kernel–Stabilizer Geometry of Observability Abstract Resolution Geometry (RG) is a protocol-explicit framework for characterizing what a declared observation system can distinguish, preserve, and consistently infer. Its starting point is a family of observation laws together with admissible outcome relabelings, rather than a covariance decomposition, metric, or dynamical model. Equality of the joint observation law defines a kernel groupoid and an observational quotient, canonically identified with the law image. An experiment-internal quantity is identifiable precisely when it is constant on observational fibres. The quotient alone determines neither a metric nor a connection, causal structure, clock, physical scale, or law of motion. The framework separates exact observational equivalence from statistical distinguishability, admissibility, symmetry, and physical realization. The stabilizer of the observation law induces a faithful effective action on the quotient. Liftable symmetry is distinguished from symmetry of the law image: the former can depend on the latent presentation, whereas the observable layer is presentation-invariant once its law-space structures and declarations are fixed. On regular strata, natural modules defined by pullback from law space descend uniquely to the observational quotient. This gives representative independence and projectability for law-defined structures, without asserting that naturality selects those structures. In regular classical experiments, the Fisher tensor supplies infinitesimal distinguishability under the stated Markov-monotonicity assumptions; its radical agrees with the observational vertical space under the corresponding regularity conditions. Quantum protocols require a declared operational task to select within the family of monotone metrics. A central organizing result concerns task-preserving conversion . For a representation map and a declared family of downstream tasks, RG characterizes the exact set of compatible task outcomes on each representation fibre. Unique inference is possible exactly when this residual is a singleton. Otherwise the appropriate output is a correspondence or a typed abstention, not an arbitrary hidden representative. Pairing a representation with its tasks gives a terminal sufficient refinement. For declared operations, observational closure is expressed by the greatest operation-stable congruence contained in the observation kernel. These constructions distinguish local differential rank, global orbit separation, observational completeness, and reconstruction, and make preservation requirements explicit under composition. Second-order realizations provide concrete classification and computational tools. Under a declared block-orthogonal gauge, a covariance datum is encoded by a symmetric matrix tuple whose ordered word traces form a complete pointwise invariant, including repeated eigenvalues, vanishing couplings, and rank-deficient sectors. On simple-spectrum strata, mixed moments recover coupling magnitudes, while independent cycle holonomies complete the residual sign classification. This distinguishes hidden values omitted by a descriptor from distinctions that are genuinely observationally null . Under the different contract of covariance-preserving block-linear transformations, canonical correlations with multiplicity classify pointwise data; constant-type families additionally carry bundle and gluing information. Pointwise classification therefore does not replace the transport, relative alignment, or global data required by field-level tasks. Across rank, symmetry, and protocol changes, RG uses specialization maps when kernel inclusion permits them and correspondences otherwise. Smooth geometry is confined to its regular domain; proper-groupoid and tame settings support stratified descriptions with slices, tangent cones, and orbit-type changes. Finite-resolution statements are separated from exact model state
items.title: Resolution Geometry of Observation Systems

items.summary: Abstract The three companions [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] use three structures side by side: probability laws and kernels, provenance (which source a record came from), and differentiation at the boundary of the simplex. This paper studies how they fit together, one layer at a time. items.summary: Continual reinforcement learning (CRL) requires agents to operate under environmental changes while reusing prior knowledge whenever possible. We argue that model-based reinforcement learning provides a promising framework for this setting because learned world models (WMs) can, in principle, support change detection, knowledge reuse, adaptation, and acquisition of new knowledge. However, such benefits depend heavily on whether the learned model can generalize beyond the contexts in which it was trained. In this work, we propose to formulate this problem with a contextual Markov decision process in which context is decomposed into behavioral and physical components. This view organizes continual WM learning into reuse, adaptation, and acquisition of new knowledge. As a first step, we study direct reuse when behavioral rules remain unchanged. Using Dyna-Q and TD-MPC in controlled FourRooms tasks, we find that zero-shot reuse can degrade substantially under physical-context changes and that this behavior depends strongly on the observation representation used by the WM. Additional ablation studies and latent-space diagnostics suggest that learned representations do not automatically provide the invariances needed for reuse. These results identify representation generalization as an important bottleneck for reliable world-model reuse in CRL.
items.title: Before We Adapt: The Zero-Shot Generalization Bottleneck in Continual World Models

items.summary: Rumor models of the Daley--Kendall and Maki--Thompson family anchor the statistical mechanics of social contagion, yet the stifler composition a rumor leaves behind has resisted closed-form analysis. Inspired by the asymmetric two-step pairing (A2SP) process of step-growth polymerization, we import its common-factor cancellation into a minimal two-stage MT variant in which re-contacted spreaders are re-activated into a senior class at rate $αk_1$ rather than stifled, and obtain exact terminal-state theorems. (i) Saturation: the rumor exhausts the ignorant pool for every stifling-to-recruitment ratio $μ>0$, with a three-way tail classification and a logarithmically critical line at $μ=1$. (ii) Final size: the terminal stifler pool splits as $(x_1,x_2)=(μ/(α+μ),α/(α+μ))$, independent of seed size; the fingerprint inverts linearly ($α=μx_2/x_1$) and matches Gillespie simulations within $0.95\%$. (iii) Pooled versus history-resolved: pooled statistics are exactly $α$-free on any static graph; only the history-resolved composition carries $α$. Restoring the classic teller-retires channel breaks the exact closure beyond quantified gates (contact rates of $1$--$3\%$ of $k_1$ for spreader channels at $μ\leq1.5$, up to $32\%$ at $μ=2$), and on configuration-model networks the composition bias decays as $\langle k\rangle^{-0.71}$. An exploratory inversion of 354,930 Higgs--Twitter retweet episodes, screened by an identity check and four negative controls, yields $\hatα=2.21\%$ (joint cluster-bootstrap CI $[1.6\%,3.0\%]$; $\approx3.7\%$ after calibration at the matched threshold). Terminal compositions identify this effective re-activation rate, an upper bound on contact-coupled re-activation; the mechanism itself requires timing information beyond the terminal state.

items.summary: Web world models increasingly predict the consequences of candidate actions before agents act, yet a plausible predicted future does not necessarily support the correct safety decision. In a matched human evaluation of 3,000 predictions from ten frozen open models, 86.1% are judged semantically plausible. However, several models exhibit highly asymmetric authorisation behaviour, combining low false-safe execution with poor recall of clarifiable ASK cases and a strong preference for BLOCK. This motivates safety sufficiency: whether a predictive interface preserves and exposes the policy-decisive information required to distinguish actions that may be EXECUTED, require clarification through ASK, or should be BLOCKED. We introduce SafeWebWorld, a benchmark for evaluating safety sufficiency across five web-safety domains through action-conditioned futures, policy-decisive evidence, and policy-conditioned decisions. Under a controlled Security-Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning protocol, evidence preservation can improve substantially while authorisation-sensitive decisions deteriorate. To determine whether this deterioration reflects loss of authorisation-sensitive score structure or a failure of the decision readout, we introduce Latent Authorisation Recovery (LAR). Frozen-score recalibration reveals substantial but backbone-dependent recovery, while paired recovery provides only a modest additional gain. Yet within-family and matched-authorisation evaluations remain poor, showing that aggregate recoverability does not imply robust fine-grained authorisation behaviour. Overall, plausible prediction, evidence preservation, and aggregate recovery are each insufficient on their own to establish robust authorisation.
items.title: Beyond Plausible Prediction: Safety Sufficiency in Web World Models

items.summary: Real-world image editing requires coordinating multiple visual transformations with content preservation and reference constraints, yet aggregate scores can readily obscure unmet local requirements. Effective evaluation must therefore identify local failures and translate them into priorities for subsequent model improvement. We introduce WeGenEditBench, comprising 2,740 evaluation instances and 148 task types across single-image, text-intensive, and multi-reference editing. Pre-generated checklists shared across models decompose each request into atomic requirements; item-level deductions and visual evidence are established first and then summarized into scores for edit execution, preservation, visual quality, and task-specific correctness. To support the experience-acquisition component of recursive self-improvement (RSI), we develop WeGenEvoStudio, a unified multi-agent harness for RSI-oriented learning that integrates model-conditioned failure diagnosis, retrieval-grounded data construction, supervised adaptation, and re-evaluation. Among 15 evaluated configurations, GPT-Image-2 leads single-image editing with an Overall score of 4.076, while Seedream-5.0-Pro leads text-intensive editing at 4.291. Evolution experiments across four generation and editing benchmarks demonstrate substantial targeted gains: on their report-selected Top-5 single-image targets, FLUX.2 [dev] improves Overall from 1.083 to 3.517, while Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 gains 13.2%. Together, our benchmark and harness provide a foundation for developing more reliable image models through interpretable evaluation and feedback-driven learning.
items.title: From Evaluation to Evolution: Benchmarking Image Editing and Evolving Image Models

items.summary: Human preferences change over time: an established preference may remain valid over time, become uncertain as context shifts, or be explicitly revised. Effective personalization requires conversational AI to adapt its response strategy to evolving preferences rather than relying on passive memory retrieval. We formalize this capability as adaptive personalization under epistemic uncertainty. A human preference study further confirms that people favor state-contingent response strategies as preference uncertainty changes. To evaluate whether language models mirror this adaptation, we create a multilingual benchmark spanning 250 personas, 5 languages, and 25K conversational turns that decouples strategy selection from response execution. Across eight closed- and open-weight models, we uncover a recognition-generation gap: models reliably identify appropriate strategies when selecting among candidate options, but collapse during open-ended generation, suffering a 35-46% drop in strategy calibration. Crucially, this failure is systematic: models default to exploit-first behavior, over-relying on existing preferences regardless of preference epistemic uncertainty. We show this failure is addressable: while prompting interventions fail, targeted training that supervises models' internal strategy representations toward state-conditional human preferences narrows the user acceptability generalization gap by a third on out-of-distribution personas and conversational styles.
items.title: Adaptive Personalization Under Preference Epistemic Uncertainty

items.summary: Iterative language-model optimizers refine prompts and programs by evaluating a candidate, showing a proposer model a sample of failing cases, and keeping revisions that improve performance. Recent work attributes the limits of this loop to narrow single-round reflection, introducing full-set error clustering, targeted minibatches, or larger proposer models so the optimizer sees more failure modes per step. Yet every existing evaluation tests these mechanisms exclusively inside lineage-preserving search, where each revision edits a surviving parent, leaving the contribution of parent inheritance confounded with the breadth of per-round feedback. Across 1,750 pre-registered runs spanning nine prompt and program synthesis benchmarks, we separate parent inheritance from feedback disclosure under matched evaluation budgets. We find that greedy parent inheritance drives the vast majority of optimization progress, outperforming seed-reset resampling even when seed-reset proposals receive a clustered summary of all failures in every round or use a larger proposer model. While full-set error clustering and diverse failure selection improve single-step rewrites from the seed and accelerate the opening rounds of search, sequential parent inheritance rapidly closes this gap as solved error modes are retained in the candidate and filtered from subsequent failure lists. Moreover, decomposing token expenditure in GEPA reveals that proposer reflection accounts for only a small fraction of total cost whereas validation and minibatch gating consume nearly the entire budget, showing that greedy parent inheritance over raw failures captures the gains of complex reflective loops at a fraction of their compute.
items.title: Lineage Is Memory: Parent Inheritance and Feedback Disclosure in Short-Budget LLM-Guided Optimization

items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents embedded in software-as-a-service (SaaS) platforms inherit the user's permissions. When a permission is revoked during a task, the platform rejects the next read, but the agent still retains the data it previously retrieved in its context, drafts, saved documents, and memory. This study examined how platforms can enforce a mid-task revocation on that working state. The author defined correct behavior for four revocation types, each mapped to an obligation to block, purge, or suspend, including leaks through paraphrases, aggregates, and existence hints. The author built RevBench, a simulated field-service platform, and compared nine enforcement designs from access control, information-flow control, and machine unlearning on six frontier models in 6,048 runs. Outputs were scored using exact matching and two large-language-model judges. Per-call authorization still failed in 417 of 720 runs (57.9%), rising from 34.4% when the revocation preceded retrieval to 72.8% when it followed delivery. Information-flow labels leaked the least (12.9%) but left revoked data saved in 44.2% of runs. Designs that invalidated the context performed best, while editing the context in place left derived facts behind. A full restart and selective replay with listing-level provenance reached 21.4% and 21.0% substantive failure, the latter with 12.1% fewer model calls. Most remaining failures were disclosures about the restriction, often repeating the platform’s own notice, and larger models did not reduce them. SaaS platforms need revocation controls that reach the agent’s working state and match the type of revocation. items.summary: Abstract: Classical inferential statistics and p-value hypothesis testing in healthcare big data repositories suffer from severe structural limitations, notably p-hacking, asymptotic N-bias, and the frequent violation of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) assumptions due to intra-patient longitudinal dependencies, hospital clustering, and epidemiological shockwaves. To overcome these failures, we introduce an Inverse Breakpoint Analysis, a scale-invariant, physics-inspired metrological audit framework. Our analysis treats discrete clinical event counts not as abstract probabilities, but as physical informational mass. Grounded in Garwood exact discrete limits and Wilson-Hilferty approximations, the framework extends our previous work on stress testing indices for Big health data and establishes three rigorous thresholds: a pure mass saturation limit, a baseline tolerance band, and a structural signal threshold. Through the use of these three parameters, our inverse break-point analysis eliminates false-positive artifacts induced by massive repository sizes while preventing under-powering in small cohorts. Ultimately, the framework demonstrates that percentage-based thresholds are kinematic artifacts of scale, whereas absolute excess discrete mass serves as the sole physical invariant for healthcare data validation. We validated this approach with numerous illustrative examples.
items.title: Inverse Breakpoint Analysis: A Scale-Invariant Physics-Inspired Metrological Audit for Sanitary Big Data

items.summary: Flapping-wing simulation must reconcile high-frequency wingbeat aerodynamics with the slower dynamics relevant to flight control and reinforcement learning. We present FlapSim, a modular open-source MuJoCo simulation platform that combines robot descriptions, wing geometry, and composable aerodynamic models in a deterministic simulation pipeline. Across $48$ held-out scenarios spanning frequency, gimbal, wind, frequency-step, gust, and cross-robot flat-plate regimes, we compare five reduced-order configurations operating at $1\,\text{ms}$ with a $50\,μ\text{s}$ quasi-steady blade-element reference. The built-in hover cycle-averaged baseline achieves a $67.51\times$ CPU speedup but only $0.6593$ mean wrench fidelity. Combining multirate $21$-substep clock synchronization, three-dimensional linear/quadratic inflow and gust coupling, analytical blade-element geometry scaling, and phase-locked $1f\text{--}6f$ harmonics raises mean fidelity to $0.9646$ at a $65.19\times$ speedup in a five-block model. A streamlined four-block model without explicit step-transient lag states achieves $0.9662$ fidelity at a $67.98\times$ speedup. Controlled ablations show that stroke harmonics are particularly important during frequency transitions, improving held-out frequency-step fidelity by $+0.3176$. Transfer-function analysis explains this effect: fixed-window cycle averaging retains harmonic contributions when the wingbeat frequency changes, so within-cycle reconstruction also improves the filtered wrench. Once phase alignment and harmonic synthesis are included, explicit transient lag states provide no additional benefit in this benchmark. These results characterize the accuracy--computation tradeoff of the aerodynamic hierarchy and identify timing, inflow, geometry, and harmonic representation as central considerations for reduced-order flapping-wing simulation.
items.title: FlapSim: A Composable MuJoCo Simulation Platform and Reduced-Order Aerodynamic Model Hierarchy for Flapping-Wing Robotics

items.summary: Web world models increasingly predict the consequences of candidate actions before agents act, yet a plausible predicted future does not necessarily support the correct safety decision. In a matched human evaluation of 3,000 predictions from ten frozen open models, 86.1% are judged semantically plausible. However, several models exhibit highly asymmetric authorisation behaviour, combining low false-safe execution with poor recall of clarifiable ASK cases and a strong preference for BLOCK. This motivates safety sufficiency: whether a predictive interface preserves and exposes the policy-decisive information required to distinguish actions that may be EXECUTED, require clarification through ASK, or should be BLOCKED. We introduce SafeWebWorld, a benchmark for evaluating safety sufficiency across five web-safety domains through action-conditioned futures, policy-decisive evidence, and policy-conditioned decisions. Under a controlled Security-Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning protocol, evidence preservation can improve substantially while authorisation-sensitive decisions deteriorate. To determine whether this deterioration reflects loss of authorisation-sensitive score structure or a failure of the decision readout, we introduce Latent Authorisation Recovery (LAR). Frozen-score recalibration reveals substantial but backbone-dependent recovery, while paired recovery provides only a modest additional gain. Yet within-family and matched-authorisation evaluations remain poor, showing that aggregate recoverability does not imply robust fine-grained authorisation behaviour. Overall, plausible prediction, evidence preservation, and aggregate recovery are each insufficient on their own to establish robust authorisation.
items.title: Beyond Plausible Prediction: Safety Sufficiency in Web World Models

items.summary: Latent world models allow reinforcement learning agents to learn policies from imagined trajectories, yet determining the optimal depth of model reliance remains a fundamental challenge. Fixed imagination horizons apply uniform prediction depths regardless of trajectory reliability, exposing target values to compounding model error or over-relying on critic approximations. We introduce density-guided bootstrap boundaries, a trajectory-dependent mechanism that adapts the depth of imagined returns using a score-informed relative density proxy. The proxy accumulates the estimated divergence of a score-corrected auxiliary field formed by a feature displacement network and a noise-conditioned score estimator along imagined paths. We propose two gating mechanisms: a hard boundary that halts return expansion at a discrete state, and a soft boundary that continuously shifts the return recursion toward critic bootstrapping. Both variants preserve boundary value estimates and apply corresponding survival weights to actor and critic losses. Formulated independently of specific dynamics models and instantiated within Dreamer V3, we prove that the resulting gated Bellman operator is a strict contraction mapping and that early bootstrapping monotonically reduces conditional target variance. We clarify the theoretical assumptions distinguishing our expansion proxy from exact path likelihoods. Across continuous-control tasks and Atari Pong, empirical evaluations show that dynamic boundary selection enhances sample efficiency and late-training performance over fixed-horizon and auxiliary-enabled baselines.
items.title: Density-Guided Bootstrap Boundaries for Latent World-Model Reinforcement Learning

items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents embedded in software-as-a-service (SaaS) platforms inherit the user's permissions. When a permission is revoked during a task, the platform rejects the next read, but the agent still retains the data it previously retrieved in its context, drafts, saved documents, and memory. This study examined how platforms can enforce a mid-task revocation on that working state. The author defined correct behavior for four revocation types, each mapped to an obligation to block, purge, or suspend, including leaks through paraphrases, aggregates, and existence hints. The author built RevBench, a simulated field-service platform, and compared nine enforcement designs from access control, information-flow control, and machine unlearning on six frontier models in 6,048 runs. Outputs were scored using exact matching and two large-language-model judges. Per-call authorization still failed in 417 of 720 runs (57.9%), rising from 34.4% when the revocation preceded retrieval to 72.8% when it followed delivery. Information-flow labels leaked the least (12.9%) but left revoked data saved in 44.2% of runs. Designs that invalidated the context performed best, while editing the context in place left derived facts behind. A full restart and selective replay with listing-level provenance reached 21.4% and 21.0% substantive failure, the latter with 12.1% fewer model calls. Most remaining failures were disclosures about the restriction, often repeating the platform’s own notice, and larger models did not reduce them. SaaS platforms need revocation controls that reach the agent’s working state and match the type of revocation. items.summary: Continual reinforcement learning (CRL) requires agents to operate under environmental changes while reusing prior knowledge whenever possible. We argue that model-based reinforcement learning provides a promising framework for this setting because learned world models (WMs) can, in principle, support change detection, knowledge reuse, adaptation, and acquisition of new knowledge. However, such benefits depend heavily on whether the learned model can generalize beyond the contexts in which it was trained. In this work, we propose to formulate this problem with a contextual Markov decision process in which context is decomposed into behavioral and physical components. This view organizes continual WM learning into reuse, adaptation, and acquisition of new knowledge. As a first step, we study direct reuse when behavioral rules remain unchanged. Using Dyna-Q and TD-MPC in controlled FourRooms tasks, we find that zero-shot reuse can degrade substantially under physical-context changes and that this behavior depends strongly on the observation representation used by the WM. Additional ablation studies and latent-space diagnostics suggest that learned representations do not automatically provide the invariances needed for reuse. These results identify representation generalization as an important bottleneck for reliable world-model reuse in CRL.
items.title: Before We Adapt: The Zero-Shot Generalization Bottleneck in Continual World Models

items.summary: The ability to integrate new information and deduce its consequences is central to learning, understanding, and reasoning in large language models (LLMs). Whether information arrives during training or in-context, models must not only store local facts, but propagate their long-range implications globally. To explore information integration in LLMs, we introduce two complementary natural language benchmarks for large-scale evaluation of deductive reasoning as a function of inference depth. The first is a formal graph benchmark enabling controlled evaluation over a wide range of graph topologies and integration tasks; the second is a knowledge composition benchmark grounded in real-world knowledge graphs. We use these benchmarks to compare knowledge integration from information encoded in context versus information encoded in model weights during pretraining, evaluating a set of open models implicitly, without chain of thought. We find that accuracy decays sharply with increased composition length for both pretrained and in-context knowledge. Information presented in-context, however, substantially outperforms deduction over information encoded in weights. These results quantify a fundamental limitation of current models with direct implications for prompt-based control of agent behavior and for continual learning strategies, and they provide a foundation for developing training, prompting, and integration methods that support deeper reasoning.
items.title: ImplicitHop: Evaluating knowledge integration across context and memory

items.summary: Natural-language skills enable large language model (LLM) agents to reuse procedures across tasks, yet most systems retrieve individual skills from a flat SkillBank without explicitly modeling the high-level strategy that governs their selection and use. We introduce TalentRL, a strategy-guided reinforcement learning framework for hierarchical routing over procedural memory. Coarse-grained talents represent recurring strategies for skill use, while fine-grained skills provide executable procedures. For each task, the policy model selects a talent that guides execution and softly prioritizes its associated skills during similarity-based retrieval. However, since task outcomes depend jointly on talent selection, retrieved skill context, and downstream execution, terminal rewards alone cannot isolate the contribution of the routing decision. TalentRL therefore trains talent routing with reward contrasts between rollouts of the same task under matched interventions on the talent-conditioned context, and optimizes downstream execution with group-relative advantages. Across seven open-domain and multi-hop question-answering benchmarks, talent-aware supervised fine-tuning improves average success rate by 7.53%, 6.71%, and 9.21% over the corresponding zero-shot baselines for Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B, respectively. Reinforcement learning further improves these SFT checkpoints by 7.58% to 9.32%, and TalentRL achieves the highest average success rate among all compared methods on all three backbones. On the agentic benchmarks ALFWorld and WebShop, TalentRL achieves the highest ALFWorld success rate (99.3%) and the highest WebShop score (90.7) among all compared methods.
items.title: TalentRL: Strategy-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Hierarchical Skill Routing

items.summary: Code and results for the paper "Leakage-Aware, Edge-Deployable Brain Tumor MRI Classification: A Latency, Accuracy and Calibration Benchmark". Motivation: Ashwini et al. (doi:10.1155/acis/2622873) note that most current brain tumor segmentation and classification methods rely on offline, static imaging and therefore do not support real-time monitoring. That paper reports results on the Kaggle Brain Tumor MRI dataset (7,023 scans: pituitary, glioma, meningioma and no tumor). This record addresses part of that gap by measuring per-image CPU latency of four classifiers, as a proxy for real-time capability, and by checking whether duplicate images inflate reported accuracy. Contents: a pipeline that audits the dataset for exact and near-duplicate images, builds naive and leakage-aware splits, fine-tunes MobileNetV3, EfficientNet-B0, ResNet50 and Inception-ResNet-v2 over three seeds, measures batch-1 CPU latency, and evaluates calibration. Folders: results (main 24 runs; 7,215 images, duplicate distance 0) and results_laptop (reduced MobileNetV3 runs; 7,200 images, duplicate distance 1). The MRI images are not included; the dataset is on Kaggle (doi:10.34740/KAGGLE/DSV/2645886). See README.md for the run order.
items.title: Code and results for: Leakage-Aware, Edge-Deployable Brain Tumor MRI Classification: A Latency, Accuracy and Calibration Benchmark

FUNCTIONAL RELEASE AND INTERLABORATORY VALIDATION OF NANOROBOT-ASSISTED TISSUE MANUFACTURING AT THE LIMIT This 777-page Research Design Working Edition in the STARLI Nano Regenerative Biomanufacturing series investigates independent physical function requalification after intersite transfer. Its scientific coupling is tissue function x release qualification x interlaboratory reproducibility. The evidence perimeter is prospective and nonclinical, using closed in-vitro systems, organ-on-chip platforms or authorized ex-vivo material; neither clinical efficacy nor autonomous human intervention is claimed. The falsifiable question is: Can a second laboratory reconstruct both functional acceptance and refusal using frozen criteria without original-author assistance? The proposed minimum demonstration is: Exchange masked tissue constructs across two sites and compare fixed release decisions under a blinded transport perturbation. Strong comparators include single-central-site endpoint tests and morphology-only release. The central competing explanation is unreported remote assistance or shared calibration that defeats nominal site independence. The noncompensatory stop rule is: the receiving lab cannot independently reproduce a decision or mature function underperforms the central baseline. Every eligible, stopped, refused and unsuccessful experiment belongs to the full denominator. Thirty conditional mathematical plates specify different analytic roles, measurements, units and blind failure tests. Eighty-two chapters contain 410 individual research investigations. Two hundred Research Gates organize twenty causal challenge families across ten primary physical observables, each with an independently read companion, concealed intervention, matched comparator, explicit rival and refusal gate. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos propose future experimental and evidence instruments. All are experimental plans rather than executed observations. The source Atlas and methodology ancestors provide reference architecture but do not establish the new integrated candidate. Source-supplied ancestry includes 10.5281/zenodo.23046134 and 10.5281/zenodo.23486020; source-associated external DOI candidates must be bibliographically checked before citation. Research Gate lexical differentiation is not proof of scientific originality. The PDF is English-only and a separate QA record states outstanding independent physics, biology and DOI verification.
